Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 67, verse 1:

The Surah of al-Mulk is Meccan, according to the consensus. It is also called al-Waqiyah (the Protector) and al-Munjiyah (the Deliverer). It has thirty verses. Al-Tirmidhi narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: A man from the Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ pitched his tent over a grave, while he did not realize that it was a grave. Then it turned out that there was a man in the grave reciting the Surah "al-Mulk" until he finished it. So he came to the Prophet ﷺ and said: "O Messenger of Allah, I pitched my tent over a grave, and I did not realize that it was a grave, and then there was a man in the grave reciting the Surah 'al-Mulk' until he finished it?" The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "It is the one that prevents (the punishment), it is the one that delivers; it delivers its reciter from the punishment of the grave." He said: "A hadith that is hasan gharib." And from him (Ibn 'Abbas) he said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "I wish that 'Blessed is He in whose hand is the dominion' (Tabaraka alladhi biyadihi al-mulk) were in the heart of every believer." It was mentioned by al-Tha'labi. And from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Prophet ﷺ said: "Indeed, a surah from the Book of Allah, which is only thirty verses, interceded for a man until it brought him out of the Fire on the Day of Resurrection and admitted him into Paradise, and it is the Surah 'Tabaraka'." It was narrated by al-Tirmidhi in its meaning, and he said in it: "A hadith that is hasan." Ibn Mas'ud said: When the deceased is placed in his grave, he is approached from the direction of his feet, and it is said: "There is no way for you over him, for he used to stand in prayer with the Surah 'al-Mulk' upon his feet." Then he is approached from the direction of his head, and his tongue says: "There is no way for you over him, for he used to recite the Surah 'al-Mulk' with me." Then he said: It is the one that prevents from the punishment of Allah, and in the Torah it is the Surah "al-Mulk"; whoever recites it in a night has indeed increased and purified (his reward). And it is narrated that whoever recites it every night, the tempter (al-Fattan) will not harm him.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Blessed is He in whose hand is the dominion, and He is over all things competent.﴾ (1)

Tabaraka (تَبارَكَ) is from the form tafa'ala of barakah (blessing), and it has been discussed before [see vol. 7, p. 223]. Al-Hasan said: it means "sanctified" (taqaddasa). It was also said: it means "endured" (dama). So He is the Everlasting, whose existence has no beginning and whose permanence has no end.

(Alladhi biyadihi al-mulk) meaning: the dominion of the heavens and the earth, in this world and the Hereafter. Ibn 'Abbas said: "In His hand is the dominion; He honors whom He wills and abases whom He wills, gives life and causes death, enriches and impoverishes, gives and withholds." Muhammad ibn Ishaq said: "For Him is the dominion of prophethood, by which He honored those who followed it and abased those who opposed it."

(Wa huwa 'ala kulli shay'in qadir) — over bestowal and retribution.

**Second, the issue concerning the verse:** Concerning His words, Exalted is He, ﴿Who created death and life﴾. It has been said that the meaning is: He created you for death and life, meaning for death in this world and life in the Hereafter. He mentioned death before life because death is closer to subjugation (al-qahr), just as He mentioned daughters before sons when He said: ﴿He bestows female [children] on whom He wills﴾ [Ash-Shura 42:49] [[See vol. 16, p. 48]]. It has also been said that He mentioned it first because it is older, since things at the beginning were in the state of death, like the sperm-drop (nutfah), dust, and the like.

Qatadah said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to say: "Allah, the Exalted, humbled the children of Adam through death, made this world a house of life and then a house of death, and made the Hereafter a house of recompense and then a house of permanence." And on the authority of Abu al-Darda', the Prophet ﷺ said: "Were it not for three things, the son of Adam would not lower his head: poverty, sickness, and death, and even with that, he would [still] turn away."

**The second issue:** As for His words ﴿death and life﴾, He mentioned death before life because the people most strongly motivated to act are those who keep their death before their eyes, so it was put first because it is more important with respect to the purpose the verse is directed toward. [This is also the wording of al-Kashshaf. The wording of al-Khatib al-Shirbini in his tafsir is: "It has been said that death was mentioned before life because whoever keeps death before his eyes has the strongest motives to act."]

The scholars said: Death is not pure non-existence or mere annihilation. Rather, it is the severing of the soul's attachment to the body and its separation from it, a barrier between the two, and a change of state and a transfer from one abode to another. Life is the opposite of this.

It is related from Ibn 'Abbas, al-Kalbi, and Muqatil that death and life are bodies: death was made in the form of a ram that does not pass by anything, nor smell its scent, without dying, and life was created in the form of a white-spotted female horse (balqa') — the one that Jibril and the prophets, peace be upon them, used to ride — whose stride is as far as the eye can see, larger than a donkey and smaller than a mule. It does not pass by anything that smells its scent without coming to life, nor does it step on anything without it coming to life. It is the same one from whose hoofprint al-Samiri took a handful and cast it upon the calf, and it came to life. This was related by al-Tha'labi and al-Qushayri from Ibn 'Abbas, and al-Mawardi transmitted its meaning from Muqatil and al-Kalbi.

I say: In the Revelation there is ﴿Say: The angel of death who has been entrusted with you will take you [in death]﴾ [As-Sajdah 32:11] [[See vol. 14, p. 93]], and ﴿If you could see when the angels take those who disbelieve [in death]﴾ [Al-Anfal 8:50] [[See vol. 8, p. 28]], then ﴿Our messengers take him [in death]﴾ [Al-An'am 6:61] [[See vol. 7, p. 7]], then He said: ﴿Allah takes the souls at the time of their death﴾ [Az-Zumar 39:42] [[See vol. 15, p. 260]]. So the intermediaries are noble angels, may the blessings of Allah be upon them. He, glory be to Him, is the Causer of death in truth, and death is only depicted as a ram in the Hereafter and slaughtered upon the Sirat, as the sound report has stated. What is mentioned from Ibn 'Abbas requires a sound report that removes all excuse. And Allah knows best.

Also from Muqatil: ﴿He created death﴾, meaning the sperm-drop (nutfah), the clinging clot ('alaqah), and the lump of flesh (mudghah); and ﴿He created life﴾, meaning He created a human being and breathed the spirit into him, so he became a human. I say: This is a good opinion, and it is indicated by His words: ﴿that He may test you as to which of you is best in deed﴾, and the discussion of this has preceded in Surah Al-Kahf [[See vol. 10, p. 395]].

As-Suddi said concerning His words, Exalted is He: ﴿Who created death and life that He may test you as to which of you is best in deed﴾, meaning: the most numerous of you in remembrance of death and the best in preparation for it, and of those, the most fearful and cautious.

Ibn 'Umar said: The Prophet ﷺ recited ﴿Blessed is He in whose hand is the dominion﴾ until he reached ﴿which of you is best in deed,﴾ and then said: "[The best is] the one most scrupulous regarding the prohibitions of Allah and quickest in obedience to Allah."

It has also been said: The meaning of ﴿that He may test you﴾ is that He deals with you in the manner of one who tests, i.e., He tests the servant with the death of one dear to him, to show his patience, and with life, to show his gratitude. It has been said: Allah created death for the resurrection and recompense, and created life for trial. So the lam in ﴿that He may test you﴾ is connected to the creation of life, not to the creation of death; this was mentioned by al-Zajjaj. Al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj also said: The trial did not fall upon ﴿ayyukum﴾ ("which of you") because between the trial and "ayyukum" there is an implied verb, as you would say: "I tested you in order to see which of you is more obedient." A similar example is His words: ﴿Ask them which of them will vouch for that﴾ [Al-Qalam 68:40] [[See p. 247 of this part]], meaning: ask them, then look which of them. So ﴿ayyukum﴾ is in the nominative as the subject (mubtada'), and ﴿ahsanu 'amalan﴾ is its predicate. The meaning is: ﴿that He may test you, so that He may know or see which of you is best in deed.﴾

**﴿And He is the Almighty﴾** in His retribution against those who disobey Him.

**﴿the Oft-Forgiving﴾** toward whoever repents.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (*al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran*) on Surah 67, verse 3:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Who created seven heavens, layered one above another﴾. That is, some of them are above others. The part that is in contact with the others is their edges; this is what is reported from Ibn Abbas. *Tibaqan* (طِباقاً) is a *na't* (adjective) of *sab'a* (سَبْعَ), so it is a description by means of a *masdar* (verbal noun). It has also been said that it is a *masdar* in the sense of *muṭabaqa* (مُطَابَقَة, "fitting closely"), meaning: He created seven heavens and layered them in layering, or in fitting closely, or as in *ṭūbiqat ṭibāqan* (طُوبِقَتْ طِبَاقاً, "they were layered in layers"). Sibawayh said: *tibaqan* is in the accusative because it is a second object (*maf'ul thani*). I say: in that case *khalaqa* (خَلَقَ) has the meaning of *ja'ala* (جَعَلَ, "made") and *sayyara* (صَيَّرَ, "rendered"). *Ṭibaq* (طِبَاقٌ) is the plural of *ṭabaq* (طَبَقٌ), like *jamal* and *jimal*. It has also been said that it is the plural of *ṭabaqa* (طَبَقَةٌ). Aban ibn Taghlib said: "I heard one of the Bedouins dispraising a man, and he said: 'His evil is layered (*ṭibaq*), and his good is not lasting.'" Outside the Quran, it is permissible to read *sab'a samawat ṭibaq* with a genitive ending (*khafḍ*) as an adjective of *samawat*. A parallel to this is ﴿and seven green ears of grain﴾ [Yusuf: 46] [[See vol. 9, p. 201]].

(﻿﻿﻿ ﻿﻿ *Ma tara fi khalqi al-Rahmani min tafawut* ﻿) The reading of Hamza and al-Kisa'i is *min tafawwut* (مِنْ تَفَوُّتٍ), without an alif and with a shadda. This is also the reading of Ibn Mas'ud and his companions. The rest read *min tafawut* (مِنْ تَفَاوُتٍ) with an alif. Both are dialectal forms (*lughatan*), like *al-ta'ahhud* and *al-ta'ahhud*, *al-tahammul* and *al-tahammul*, *al-tazahhur* and *al-tazahur*, *tasaghhur* and *tasaghur*, *tada'uf* and *tada'uf*, *tabaʻud* and *tabaʻud*; all have the same meaning. Abu Ubayd preferred *min tafawwut* and argued from the hadith of Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Bakr: "Is it me that someone would act against in regard to his daughters?!" [[That is, he would act in two matters without his permission. He said this when he learned that his sister, Sayyida Aisha, had married off his son while he was absent, to al-Mundhir ibn al-Zubayr. The wording of the hadith is: "Amthali yuf'al bi-fatat" instead of "yutafawwat."]] Al-Nahhas said: This view is rejected against Abu Ubayd, because *yutafawwat* means *yuftat* (يُفْتَاتُ, "is acted upon without consent") regarding them, whereas *tafawut* in the verse is closer in sense. Just as it is said *tabayana* (تَبَايَنَ, "differed"), it is also said *tafawata al-amr* (تَفَاوَتَ الْأَمْرُ) when it differs and is far apart, i.e., one part of it falls short of another. Do you not see that before it is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Who created seven heavens, layered one above another﴾? The meaning is: you see no crookedness, no inconsistency, and no discrepancy in the creation of the Most Merciful; rather, it is straight and even, indicating its Creator, even though its forms and attributes differ. It has also been said that the intended meaning is the heavens specifically, i.e., you see no defect in the creation of the heavens. Its root is from *fawt* (فَوْتٌ, "escape, failure"), which is that one thing escapes another, so that a flaw arises from its lack of evenness. Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, supports this with his saying: "one who is scattered (*tafarraqa*)." Abu Ubayda said: it is said *tafawwata al-shay'* (تَفَوَّتَ الشَّيْءَ), meaning *fat* (فَاتَ, "it escaped").

Then He commanded them to look at His creation so that they might take lesson from it and reflect on His power. He said: (﻿﻿ *Thumma irji' al-basara hal tara min futur* ﻿﻿) That is: return your gaze to the sky. It is also said: turn the gaze over in the sky. And it is said: strain your sight toward the sky. The meanings are close. He said *fa-irji'* (فَارْجِعِ) with the *fa* (فَ), although there is no verb mentioned before it, because He had said *ma tara* (مَا تَرَى, "you do not see"). The meaning is: look, then return the gaze, do you see any *futur* (فُطُورٌ)? This was said by Qatada. *Futur* means cracks (*shuquq*), according to Mujahid and al-Dahhak. Qatada said: it means flaws (*khalal*). Al-Suddi said: it means holes (*khurug*). Ibn Abbas said: it means weakness (*wahn*). Its root is from *tafattur* (تَفَطُّرٌ) and *infitar* (اِنْفِطَارٌ), which is splitting (*inshiqaq*). The poet said:

*He built for you a sky without pillars,*
*and adorned it, and there is no flaw (*futur*) in it.*

Another said:

*You split the heart, then you scattered into it*
*your love, so it was wounded, and the wound (*futur*) closed.*

*It penetrated where no drink reached,*
*nor intoxication, nor did joy reach it.*

The Almighty's words: ﴿Then turn your gaze again, twice﴾. "Karratayn" (twice) is in the accusative of the verbal noun, because its meaning is "rajʿatayn" (returning twice), that is, one time after another. He commanded looking twice because a person who looks at a thing once does not see its flaw unless he looks at it a second time. So Allah informs us that even if one looks at the sky twice, he will see no flaw in it, but will instead be bewildered by looking at it. This is the meaning of His words: ﴿the gaze will return to you, dazed (khāsiʾan), and it will be weary﴾. "Khāsiʾan" means humbled, abased, and distanced from seeing anything of that kind. It is said: "khasaʾtu al-kalb," meaning I drove away the dog and expelled it. "Khasaʾa al-kalbu" by itself can be transitive and intransitive, and "inkhasaʾa al-kalb" is also used. "Khasaʾa baṣaruhu khasʾan wa khusūʾan" means his sight was dazzled, that is, he could hardly see. From this is His saying: ﴿the gaze will return to you, dazed﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "al-khāsiʾ is the one who did not see what he desired."

﴿And it is weary (ḥasīr)﴾: meaning it has reached the utmost limit of fatigue. So it is in the sense of the active participle, from "al-ḥusūr," which is fatigue. It may also be a passive participle from "ḥasarahu buʿd al-shayʾ" (the distance of a thing exhausted him), and this is the meaning of Ibn ʿAbbas's statement. From this is the words of the poet:

"Whoever extends his gaze beyond its limit,
his gaze returns dazed, and it has become exhausted."

It is said: "qad ḥasara baṣaruhu yaḥsiru ḥusūran," meaning his sight tired and its looking ceased from long reaching and the like. So he is "ḥasīr" and also "maḥsūr." He said:

"I looked at her in al-Muḥaṣṣab of Mina,
so my gaze returned to me, and it was weary."

Another said, describing a she-camel:

"Toward her side is a gaze of two eyes that is exhausted."
[[This is the second half of a line by Qays ibn Khuwaylid al-Hudhali. Its first half is:
"Indeed, the restlessness with her is a disease that clings to her."
And "al-ʿasīr" is the she-camel that has not been tamed (not made submissive).]]

"Shaṭrahā" is in the accusative as an adverb of place, meaning toward her. Another said:

"And the horses are disheveled, their mares never cease,
weary, leaving their foals on the road."

It was also said that "ḥasīr" means regretful. From this is the words of the poet:

"I am not today in a state of what has passed,
O daughter of the smith, you have turned back in regret."

The intended meaning of "karratayn" here is multiplicity. The evidence for this is: ﴿the gaze will return to you, dazed, and it will be weary﴾, and this is evidence of the abundance of looking.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 67, verses 5–6:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We have adorned the lowest heaven with lamps﴾. *Masabih* is the plural of *misbah*, which means a lamp. The stars are also called *masabih* because of their shining.

(And We have made them *rujum*) That is, We have made their meteors (*shuhub*), so the word for the thing is omitted and the word for its source stands in its place.

Its evidence is ﴿Except one who snatches a fragment, and is pursued by a piercing flame﴾ [al-Saffat: 10]. (See vol. 15, p. 66.) On this view, the lamps do not move and are not hurled. It has also been said that the pronoun refers to the lamps, on the basis that the hurling comes from the stars themselves, and that the star does not fall; rather, a part of it breaks off and is hurled, without its light or its form being diminished. This was said by Abu Ali, in answer to someone who said: How can they be an adornment when they are missiles that do not remain? Al-Mahdawi said: This is on the basis that the eavesdropping (*isti'raq*) takes place from the position of the stars. The first explanation is on the basis that the eavesdropping takes place from the air, which is below the position of the stars. Al-Qushayri said: A better view than Abu Ali's is that we say: they are an adornment before the devils are pelted with them.

*Rujum* is the plural of *rajm*, which is a verbal noun used to name that with which something is pelted. Qatada said: God created the stars for three purposes: as an adornment for the sky, as missiles against the devils, and as signs by which one is guided on land, at sea, and in determining times. Whoever interprets them otherwise has burdened himself with what he has no knowledge of, has overstepped, and has done wrong. Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: By God, none of the people of the earth has a star in the sky, but they take soothsaying (*kihana*, divination) as a path and take the stars as a pretext.

(And We have prepared for them the punishment of the Blaze) That is, We have prepared for the devils the most severe burning. It is said: The fire was kindled (*su'irat*), so it is *masjurah* and *sa'ir*, like *maqtulah* and *qatil*.

(And for those who disbelieve in their Lord is the punishment of Jahannam, and it is an evil destination) ﴿And for those who disbelieve in their Lord is the punishment of Jahannam, and wretched is the destination﴾.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 67, verse 7:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿When they are thrown into it﴾, meaning the disbelievers.

(They hear from it a roaring) i.e., a sound. Ibn 'Abbas said: The roaring belongs to Jahannam at the moment the disbelievers are cast into it; it heaves toward them with a heave like the heaving of a mule toward barley, then it exhales an exhalation such that no one remains who is not terrified. It was also said: the roaring comes from the disbelievers when they are cast into the Fire; this was related by 'Ata'. The shahiq (inhaling sob) is in the chest, and the zafir (exhaling roar) is in the throat. This has already passed in surah Hud [[see vol. 9, p. 98]].

(While it boils up) i.e., it seethes. From this is the verse of Hassan:

You left your cooking pot with nothing in it, / but the pot of the people is hot and boiling.

Mujahid said: It boils with them as a small amount of grain boils in a large quantity of water. Ibn 'Abbas said: It seethes with them over the cauldron, and this is from the intensity of the flame of the Fire and the intensity of anger, just as you say, "So-and-so is seething with rage."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 67, verses 8–11:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Almost bursting with fury﴾. He means: they would be cut off and separate from one another. This is what Sa'id ibn Jubayr said. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Dahhak and Ibn Zayd said: they would scatter apart. ﴿With fury﴾ means: from the intensity of the rage against the enemies of Allah, exalted is He. It was also said: "with fury" means from boiling. The original form of tamayyazu is tatamayyazu.

(Every time a group) is cast into it, that is, a company of the disbelievers.

(Its keepers ask them) in a manner of reproach and rebuke: (Did no warner come to you?) That is, a messenger in the world who warned you of this day, so that you would take heed.

(They say: Yes indeed, a warner came to us) who warned us and frightened us.

(But we denied and said: Allah has not sent down anything.) That is, through your tongues.

(You are only in great error.) That is, O company of messengers.

They acknowledged their denial of the messengers, then they acknowledged their own ignorance, saying while they were in the Fire: (Had we listened) to the warners, meaning the messengers, to what they brought, (or used our reason) concerning them. Ibn 'Abbas said: Had we listened to guidance or understood it, or had we listened the listening of one who comprehends and reflects, or used reason as one who discerns and considers. This indicates that the disbeliever has been given no portion of reason. Its explanation has already passed in "al-Tur" [see vol. 17, p. 73], and praise be to Allah.

(We would not have been among the companions of the Blaze.) That is, we would not have been among the people of the Fire.

It is narrated from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The wicked will regret on the Day of Resurrection. They will say: Had we listened or used reason, we would not have been among the companions of the Blaze." Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿So they acknowledged their sin﴾, that is, their denial of the messengers. The word "sin" (dhanb) here carries the sense of a collective, because it has the meaning of an act. It is said: "the gifts (ʿaṭa') of the people went out", meaning their gifts.

(So away with the companions of the Blaze!) That is, far away they are from the mercy of Allah. Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Abu Salih said: it is a valley in Hell called al-Suhq. Al-Kisa'i and Abu Ja'far read fa-suhqan with a dammah on the ha', and it was also transmitted from 'Ali. The rest read it with a sukun on it; both are dialects, like al-suht and al-ru'b. al-Zajjaj said: it is in the accusative as a verbal noun, meaning: Allah made them far away, that is, removed them to a distance. Imru' al-Qays said:

It wanders among the far borders of the lands, and the breeze of the east wind drives it away, every driving.

Abu 'Ali said: the analogical form would be ishqan, but the verbal noun came in the elided form, as it is said: "and if I perish, that was my destiny" (qadri), meaning my decree.

It was also said that the words of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿You are only in great error﴾ are the words of the keepers of Hell to its inhabitants.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 67, verses 8–11:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Almost bursting with fury﴾. He means: they would be cut off and separate from one another. This is what Sa'id ibn Jubayr said. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Dahhak and Ibn Zayd said: they would scatter apart. ﴿With fury﴾ means: from the intensity of the rage against the enemies of Allah, exalted is He. It was also said: "with fury" means from boiling. The original form of tamayyazu is tatamayyazu.

(Every time a group) is cast into it, that is, a company of the disbelievers.

(Its keepers ask them) in a manner of reproach and rebuke: (Did no warner come to you?) That is, a messenger in the world who warned you of this day, so that you would take heed.

(They say: Yes indeed, a warner came to us) who warned us and frightened us.

(But we denied and said: Allah has not sent down anything.) That is, through your tongues.

(You are only in great error.) That is, O company of messengers.

They acknowledged their denial of the messengers, then they acknowledged their own ignorance, saying while they were in the Fire: (Had we listened) to the warners, meaning the messengers, to what they brought, (or used our reason) concerning them. Ibn 'Abbas said: Had we listened to guidance or understood it, or had we listened the listening of one who comprehends and reflects, or used reason as one who discerns and considers. This indicates that the disbeliever has been given no portion of reason. Its explanation has already passed in "al-Tur" [see vol. 17, p. 73], and praise be to Allah.

(We would not have been among the companions of the Blaze.) That is, we would not have been among the people of the Fire.

It is narrated from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The wicked will regret on the Day of Resurrection. They will say: Had we listened or used reason, we would not have been among the companions of the Blaze." Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿So they acknowledged their sin﴾, that is, their denial of the messengers. The word "sin" (dhanb) here carries the sense of a collective, because it has the meaning of an act. It is said: "the gifts (ʿaṭa') of the people went out", meaning their gifts.

(So away with the companions of the Blaze!) That is, far away they are from the mercy of Allah. Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Abu Salih said: it is a valley in Hell called al-Suhq. Al-Kisa'i and Abu Ja'far read fa-suhqan with a dammah on the ha', and it was also transmitted from 'Ali. The rest read it with a sukun on it; both are dialects, like al-suht and al-ru'b. al-Zajjaj said: it is in the accusative as a verbal noun, meaning: Allah made them far away, that is, removed them to a distance. Imru' al-Qays said:

It wanders among the far borders of the lands, and the breeze of the east wind drives it away, every driving.

Abu 'Ali said: the analogical form would be ishqan, but the verbal noun came in the elided form, as it is said: "and if I perish, that was my destiny" (qadri), meaning my decree.

It was also said that the words of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿You are only in great error﴾ are the words of the keepers of Hell to its inhabitants.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 67, verse 12:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who fear their Lord unseen﴾. Its counterpart is: "Whoever fears the Most Merciful unseen" [Qaf 50:33]. The discussion of it has already passed [see vol. 17, p. 20], namely: they fear Allah, and they fear His punishment, which is unseen, and it is the punishment of the Day of Resurrection.

(For them is forgiveness) for their sins (and a great reward), which is Paradise.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 67, verses 13–14:

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Whether you conceal your speech or disclose it﴾. The wording is that of a command, but the intended meaning is a statement of fact. That is, whether you conceal your words about the matter of Muhammad (ﷺ) or disclose them, ﴿indeed He is All-Knowing of what is within the breasts﴾, meaning of what is in the hearts of good and evil.

Ibn Abbas said: It was revealed concerning the polytheists who used to disparage the Prophet (ﷺ), and Jibril (peace be upon him) would inform him. Some of them said to others: "Conceal your speech so that the Lord of Muhammad does not hear." So it was revealed: ﴿And conceal your speech or disclose it﴾. That is: conceal your speech about the matter of Muhammad (ﷺ). It was also said that it refers to all speech. ﴿Or disclose it﴾: make it public.

﴿Indeed He is All-Knowing of what is within the breasts﴾. "Dhat al-sudur" means what is in them, just as a woman's child in her womb is called "dha batniha" (the one in her belly). Then He said: ﴿Should He not know, He who created?﴾ That is: should not the One who created the secret know the secret? He says: I created the secret in the heart, so should I not be knowing of what is in the hearts of the servants?

The scholars of meanings (Ahl al-Ma'ani) said: If you wish, make "man" (who) a name for the Creator, exalted and mighty, and the meaning will be: Should not the Creator know His creation? And if you wish, make it a name for the created, and the meaning will be: Should Allah not know whoever He created? It is necessary that the Creator knows what He created and what He creates.

Ibn al-Musayyab said: A man was standing at night among many trees, and the wind had blown strongly, and it occurred to the man's mind: "Does God know which of these leaves falls?" Then he was called from the side of the thicket [[al-ghaydah: the dense, intertwined trees]] with a mighty voice: ﴿Should He not know, He who created, and He is the Subtle, the All-Aware?﴾

Al-Ustadh Abu Ishaq al-Isfarayini said: Among the names that are attributes of the Essence (sifat al-dhat) are those pertaining to knowledge. Among them is "Al-'Alim" (the All-Knowing), whose meaning is the comprehensiveness of all objects of knowledge. Among them is "Al-Khabir" (the All-Aware), which is specific to knowing what will be before it comes to be. Among them is "Al-Hakim" (the All-Wise), which is specific to knowing the finest details of attributes. Among them is "Al-Shahid" (the All-Witnessing), which is specific to knowing the absent and the present, and its meaning is that nothing is hidden from Him. Among them is "Al-Hafiz" (the Preserver), which is specific to His not forgetting. Among them is "Al-Muhsi" (the All-Counting), which is specific to His not being preoccupied by multiplicity from knowledge, such as the light of the lamp, the intensity of the wind, and the falling of leaves; He knows at that moment the parts of the movements in every single leaf. And how would He not know, when He is the One who creates! Indeed He has said: ﴿Should He not know, He who created, and He is the Subtle, the All-Aware?﴾

**Al-Qurtubi's commentary (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 67, verse 15:**

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿He it is who made the earth subservient to you﴾, meaning easy, so that you can settle upon it. *Dhalul* means tractable, submissive to you, and its verbal noun is *dhull*, which means softness and submission. That is, He did not make the earth such that walking across it is prevented by roughness and harshness. It was also said: meaning He made it firm with mountains so that it would not shake with its inhabitants. Had it been swaying and tilting, it would not have been submissive to us. It was also said: it points to the ability to plant, to sow, to dig springs and rivers, and to dig wells.

(﴿So walk in its broad paths﴾) This is an *amr ibahah* (a command of permissibility), and it expresses the favour (of Allah). It was also said: it is a statement in the form of a command, meaning "so that you may walk in its edges, its regions, its hills and its mountains." Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah and Bashir ibn Ka'b said: *manakibiha* means its mountains. It is narrated that Bashir ibn Ka'b had a concubine, and he said to her: "If you tell me what the *manakib* of the earth are, you will be free." She said: "Its *manakib* are its mountains." So she became free, and he wished to marry her, so he asked Abu al-Darda', who said: "Leave what makes you doubtful for what does not make you doubtful." Mujahid said: *manakibiha* means its edges. He also said: its roads and its mountain passes. This was also said by al-Suddi and al-Hasan. Al-Kalbi said: its sides. The two *manakib* of a man are his two sides. The root of *al-mankib* is "side," and from it comes *mankib* of a man (the shoulder). And there is *al-rih al-nakba'* (the wind from a side direction). And so-and-so *tanakkaba* from so-and-so (he avoided him). The meaning is: walk wherever you wish, for We have made it tractable for you, not preventing you. Qatadah related from Abu al-Jald that the earth is twenty-four thousand farsakh: the Sudan have twelve thousand, the Romans eight thousand, the Persians three thousand, and the Arabs one thousand.

(﴿And eat of His provision﴾) That is, of what He has made lawful for you. This was said by al-Hasan. It was also said: of what He has brought to you.

(﴿And to Him is the resurrection﴾) That is, the return. It was also said: its meaning is that the One who created the heaven, with no discrepancy in it, and made the earth tractable, is able to resurrect you.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 67, verse 16:

Ibn ʿAbbas said: "Are you secure from the One who is in the heaven, [that He might cause the earth to swallow you] if you disobey Him?" It has also been said: the implied meaning is, "Are you secure from the One in the heaven: His power, His authority, His Throne and His dominion?" He specified the heaven, although His dominion encompasses everything, as a reminder that the God whose power takes effect in the heaven is not the one they revere on earth. It has also been said that this refers to the angels. And it has been said that it refers to Jibril, who is the angel entrusted with punishment. [Note: the word "al-ʿadhab" (the punishment) is missing from ḥ, s, h.]

I say: it is also possible that the meaning is: "Are you secure from the Creator of the One who is in the heaven, that He might cause the earth to swallow you as He swallowed Qarun?"

﴿Then, behold, it sways﴾, i.e., it goes back and forth. Al-mawr means agitation through going and coming. The poet said:

They shot, and struck the hearts true, and you will not see
Blood gushing forth except that it flows into the chests.

The plural of ḥaywum, which is the middle of the chest. When a person is swallowed by the earth, the earth turns with him, and that is al-mawr. The scholars who verify said: "Are you secure from the One who is above the heaven," like His saying: ﴿So travel freely in the land﴾ [al-Tawbah: 2], meaning above it, not by contact or confinement, but by domination and governance. It has also been said: its meaning is "Are you secure from the One who is over the heaven," like the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And I will crucify you on the trunks of palm trees﴾ [Ta-Ha: 71], meaning upon them. Its meaning is that He is its manager and owner, just as one says: "So-and-so is over Iraq and the Hijaz," meaning its governor and commander. The reports on this subject are numerous, authentic and widespread, pointing to the exaltedness [of Allah], and none rejects them except a heretic or a stubborn ignorant. Their purpose is to honour Him and to declare Him free of being below or beneath. His attribute of exaltedness and greatness is not [to be understood] in terms of places, directions or limits, because these are attributes of bodies. Hands are raised in supplication toward the heaven because the heaven is the place of descent of revelation, the abode of rain, the locus of holiness, and the source of the purified angels, and to it the deeds of the servants ascend; above it is His Throne and His Paradise. Just as Allah made the Kaʿbah a direction for supplication and prayer, [the raising of hands is for these reasons], and because He created places while He is not in need of them, and He was in His eternity before the creation of place and time. He has no place and no time, and He is now as He was.

Qunbul, on the authority of Ibn Kathir, recited ﴿al-nushur﴾ and ﴿a-amintum﴾ with the first hamza changed to a waw and the second lightened. The Kufans, the Basrans and the people of Syria, except Abu ʿAmr and Hisham, recited both hamzas with lightening, and the rest lightened [only the second]. All of this has already been mentioned.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 67, verse 17:

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿Or are you secure that He who is in the heaven will not send upon you a violent wind (ḥāṣiban)?﴾ That is, stones from the sky, as He sent them upon the people of Lot and the companions of the Elephant (aṣḥāb al-fīl). It was also said: a wind containing stones and pebbles. And it was said: a cloud containing stones.

﴿So you will know how My warning was﴾ That is, My warning (indhārī). It was also said: nadhīr here means in the sense of mundhir (the one who warns). That is, Muhammad (ﷺ). ﴿So you will know⁠⁠⁠⁠ his truthfulness and the outcome of your denial.﴾

**The Qur'an: "And those before them did indeed deny; so how was My rejection [of them]!"** (67:18)

Its meaning: "Those before them" refers to the disbelievers of earlier nations, such as the people of Noah, ʿĀd, Thamūd, the people of Lot, the companions of Madyan, the companions of al-Rass, and the people of Pharaoh.

(So how was My nakīr?) That is, My rejection (*inkārī*), and this has already been discussed [[see vol. 12, p. 73]]. Warsh affirmed the yāʾ (the final long vowel "ī") in *nadhīrī* and *nakīrī* in connected recitation (*waṣl*). Yaʿqūb affirmed it in both pausal and connected reading. The rest of the readers omitted it, following the Muṣḥaf (the ʿUthmānic codex).

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 67, verse 19:

His saying, exalted is He: "Have they not seen the birds above them, spreading their wings and folding them?" That is: just as He made the earth subservient to the son of Adam, He made the air subservient to the birds. "Spreading their wings" (ṣāffāt) means extending their wings in the air while flying, because when they spread them they arrange their feathers in rows (ṣaffa). "And folding them" (yaqbiḍna) means they strike their sides with them.

Abu Ja'far al-Nahhas said: It is said of a bird when it spreads its wings: ṣāff (ṣāffun). When it folds them so that they touch its side: qābiḍ (qābiḍun), because it folds them.

Abu Khirash said:

*yubādiru junḥa al-layli fa-huwa mawā'il*
*... yaḥuththu al-janāḥa bi-l-tabassuṭi wa-l-qabḍi*

(He hastens toward the wing of the night, and he is seeking refuge; he urges his wing with spreading and folding.)

[[As written in the manuscript copies of the original. Wāʾala al-ṭāʾir: took refuge and escaped. Wa-ila al-makān: hastened. But what is in the Diwan of the Hudhalī poets and the lexicons is: "fa-huwa mahābidh," and al-mahābadhah means haste.]]

Some say: "and folding" (wa-yaqbiḍna) refers to their wings after spreading them, when they stop flying. It is coordinated with ṣāffāt, with the present-tense verb (yaqbiḍna) coordinated onto the active participle (ṣāffāt), just as the active participle is coordinated onto the present-tense verb in the words of the poet:

*bāta yu'ashshīhā bi-'aḍbin bātirin ... yaqṣidu fī asw'uqihā wa-jā'iri*

(He spent the night feeding them with a sharp, cutting sword ... aiming at their shins and [the one who] oppresses.)

[[Its speaker is unknown, and it is in the hexameter meter (rajaz musaddas). Yu'ashshīhā: feeds them the evening meal. It is also narrated as yughashshīhā with a ghayn, from ghashāʾ, like a covering, meaning it covers them and includes them all. The feminine pronoun refers to camels, and it is in praise of a generous man who hastened to slaughter his camels for his guests. ʿAḍb: sword. Yaqṣidu: from qaṣd, which is the opposite of injustice. Asw'uq: plural of sāq, the part between the knee and the foot. Jā'ir: from jāra, to act unjustly, i.e., he oppresses.

(See Khizanat al-Adab on the 356th poetic citation.)]]

"What holds them up" means: nothing holds the birds up in the air while they fly except Allah, mighty and majestic. "Indeed He is All-Seeing of everything."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 67, verse 20:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Or who is it that can be a host (jund) for you, to help you, apart from the Most Merciful?﴾ Ibn 'Abbas said: a party (hizb) and a protection (mana'ah) for you.

﴿He would help you apart from the Most Merciful﴾, so that He would ward off from you what He wills to inflict upon you if you disobey Him. The word jund (host, army) is used in the singular form, and for this reason He said: ﴿who is it that is a host for you﴾. This is a rhetorical question of denial, meaning: there is no host for you that can ward off the punishment of God from you, apart from the Most Merciful, i.e., other than the Most Merciful.

﴿The disbelievers are only in delusion﴾ caused by the devils, who deceive them into thinking that there is no punishment and no reckoning.

The Almighty's saying: ﴿Or who is this that provides for you?﴾ That is, who gives you the benefits of this world. It was also said: "the rain is from your gods."

(﴿If He withholds His provision﴾) meaning, Allah the Exalted withholds His provision.

(﴿Nay, they persist﴾) that is, they persevere and insist.

(﴿in obstinate arrogance﴾) in rebellion (ʿutuww, transgression), (﴿and aversion﴾) from the truth.

**[The text between the two square brackets is omitted from manuscripts S and H.]**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Is one who walks prone upon his face...﴾. Allah struck a parable for the believer and the disbeliever. *Mukibban* means one who has lowered his head, not looking ahead of him, nor to his right, nor to his left. So he is not safe from stumbling and falling on his face. This is like one who walks upright, balanced, looking at what is before him, to his right, and to his left.

Ibn 'Abbas said: "This refers to the world." It is also possible that it refers to the blind man who cannot find the way and so wanders aimlessly (*i'tisaf*, meaning to travel through a desert and cross it without purpose or guidance, and without aiming for any intended destination or any established road). Such a person keeps falling on his face. He is not like the upright, healthy, sighted man walking on a road he has been guided to.

Qatadah said: "It is the disbeliever who devoted himself (*akkaba*) to acts of disobedience to Allah in the world, so Allah will gather him on the Day of Resurrection upon his face."

Ibn 'Abbas and al-Kalbi said: "By the one who walks prone upon his face, He means Abu Jahl, and by the one who walks upright, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)." It has also been said that it means Abu Bakr, and it has been said that it means Hamzah, and it has been said that it means 'Ammar ibn Yasir, as 'Ikrimah stated.

It has also been said: it is general, applying to both the disbeliever and the believer. That is, the disbeliever does not know whether he is upon the truth or upon falsehood, that is, whether this disbeliever is more rightly guided, or the Muslim who walks upright and balanced, seeing the way, and he is upon a straight path, which is Islam.

It is said: *akabba al-rajulu 'ala wajhihi* (the man fell upon his face), used without the *alif* when it is intransitive. When it is transitive, it is said: *kabbahu Allahu li-wajhihi* (Allah made him fall upon his face), without the *alif*.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 67, verse 23:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: It is He who brought you into being⦆ He commanded His Prophet to make them aware of the ugliness of their polytheism, along with their acknowledgment that Allah created them.

(And He made for you hearing and sight and hearts) meaning the hearts (little is it that you give thanks) i.e. you do not give thanks for these blessings, and you do not affirm the oneness of Allah, exalted is He. One says: "qalama af'alu kadha" (I rarely do such a thing), meaning: I do not do it.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 67, verse 24–25:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Say: It is He who created you (dhara'akum) in the earth﴾, meaning: He created you in the earth, as Ibn 'Abbas said. And it was said: He scattered you in it and dispersed you over its surface, as Ibn Shajara said.

(And to Him you will be gathered) so that He may recompense each one for his deeds.

(And they say: When is this promise, if you are truthful?) meaning: When is the Day of Resurrection? And when is this punishment with which you threaten us? This is mockery on their part. It has already been mentioned [see vol. 8, p. 349].

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 67, verse 26:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Say: The knowledge is only with Allah﴾, meaning: Say to them, O Muhammad, that knowledge of the time of the Hour is with Allah, so none other than Him knows it. Its parallel is: ﴿Say: Its knowledge is only with my Lord﴾ [al-A'raf: 187], and the verse continues [[see vol. 7, p. (335)]].

﴿And I am only a warner, clear﴾, meaning: one who gives warning and instructs you.

Al-Qurtubi's commentary on Surah 67, verse 27:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿When they see it [coming] near﴾. "Zulfah" is a verbal noun meaning "close" (mazdalafan), that is, "near." This is the view of Mujahid. Al-Hasan said it means "face to face" (ʿiyanan). Most exegetes (mufassirun) hold that the meaning is: when they see it, that is, the punishment, which is the punishment of the Hereafter. Mujahid said: it means the punishment of Badr. It was also said: they saw what they had been promised of the gathering (al-hashr) close to them, and the words ﴿you will be gathered﴾ point to this. Ibn ʿAbbas said: when they saw their evil deeds near them.

﴿Then the faces of those who disbelieved will be evil﴾, that is, evil was done to them. Al-Zajjaj said: evil appears in them, meaning that punishment distressed them and a mark showing their disbelief appeared on their faces, like His saying, the Exalted: ﴿On the Day when some faces turn white and some faces turn black﴾ [Al ʿImran: 106] [See vol. 4, p. 166].

Nafiʿ, Ibn Muhaysin, Ibn ʿAmir and al-Kisaʾi read "suʾat" with ishmam (a slight rounding of the lips toward the ḍamma, an articulation called ishmam, "the admixture of the vowel"). The rest read it with a kasra and without ishmam, seeking lightness. Whoever reads with a ḍamma is observing the original form.

﴿And it will be said: This is what you used to call for﴾. Al-Farraʾ said: "tadduʿūn" is "taftaʿilūn" from the root "duʿāʾ," and this is the view of most scholars, meaning: you used to wish for and ask for.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: "you used to lie." Its interpretation is: this is what, on account of which, you used to claim falsehoods and fabrications, as al-Zajjaj said. The common reading (qiraʾat al-ʿammah) is "tadda'ūn" with shaddah, and its interpretation is what we have mentioned. Qatadah, Ibn Abi Ishaq, al-Dahhak and Yaʿqub read "tadʿūn" without shaddah. Qatadah said: it refers to their saying, ﴿Our Lord, hasten to us our share [of punishment] before the Day of Reckoning﴾ [Sad: 16] [See vol. 15, p. 157]. Al-Dahhak said: it refers to their saying, ﴿O Allah, if this is the truth from You, then rain down upon us stones from the sky﴾ [Al-Anfal: 32], and so on (the verse) [See vol. 7, p. 398].

Abu al-ʿAbbas said: "tadda'ūn" means "tastaʿjilūn" (you hasten). It is said: "daʿawtu bi-kadha" when I sought it, and "idda'aytu" is its "ifta'altu" form. Al-Nahhas said: "tadda'ūn" and "tadʿūn" have one meaning, as it is said "qadara" and "iqtadara," and "ʿadā" and "iʿtadā." However, in the form "ifta'ala" there is the sense of one thing after another, while "fa'ala" applies to both the little and the much.

Allah's words: "Say: Have you considered if Allah destroys me" — that is, "say to them, O Muhammad" (the "ay" here is explanatory; the word "ay" is omitted in manuscripts ḥ and s). He means the polytheists of Makkah, who used to wish for the death of Muhammad (ﷺ), as Allah says: "Or do they say, 'A poet, we await for him the misfortune of time'" (al-Tur 52:30). [See vol. 17, p. 71.]

"Have you considered, if we die or Allah has mercy on us and our terms are delayed, who will protect you from the punishment of Allah? There is no need for you to wait for us or to hasten the coming of the Hour."

Ibn Muhaysin, al-Musayyabi, Shaybah, al-A'mash and Hamzah pronounced the yā' in "ahlakanī" with sukūn (silent). The rest read it with fatḥah. All of them read the yā' in "wa man maʿiya" with fatḥah, except the people of Kufa, who read it with sukūn. Ḥafs read it with fatḥah, like the majority.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 67, verse 29:

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Say, "He is the Most Merciful. We have believed in Him, and upon Him we have relied. So you will know who it is that is in clear error."﴾ Al-Kisa'i (ي) read it with the ya' (fa-sa-ya'lamun), as a report, and he transmitted it from Ali. The rest read it with the ta' (fa-sa-ta'lamun), as direct address. And it is a threat to them.

It is said: Why did he place the object of "amanna" (we believed) later and place the object of "tawakkalna" (we relied) earlier? It is said: it is because "amanna" falls as an implicit contrast with the disbelievers, since it comes right after mentioning them, as if it were said: "We believed and did not disbelieve as you disbelieved." Then he said, "and upon Him we have relied," specifically: "we do not rely upon what you rely upon of your men and your wealth." This is what al-Zamakhshari said.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 67, verse 30:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: Have you considered?﴾ O assembly of Quraysh. (If your water should become gone (ghawran)), i.e., sunk away into the earth, so that buckets cannot reach it. Their water came from two wells: the well of Zamzam and the well of Maymun.

(Then who will bring you clear water?) i.e., flowing water. This was said by Qatadah and al-Dahhak. They must therefore say: "Only Allah brings it to us." So say to them: "Why do you associate with Him those who cannot bring you [water]?" It is said: ghara al-ma' yaghuru ghawran, meaning it receded and dried up. Al-ghawr means "the sunken," and it is described with the verbal noun for emphasis, as you say: "a man who is ʿadl (just) and riḍan (content)." This has already been discussed in surah "al-Kahf" [[See vol. 10, p. (409)]], and the meaning was discussed in surah "al-Mu'minun" [[See vol. 2, p. (112)]], and praise be to Allah. From Ibn ʿAbbas: "bi-ma'in ma'in" means apparent, which the eyes can see, so it is in the sense of maf'ul (passive). It is also said that it derives from maʿana al-ma', meaning it became abundant, and on this view it is of the form faʿil. Also from Ibn ʿAbbas: the meaning is "then who will bring you sweet water." And Allah knows best. [[In manuscript H: The surah was completed, and praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds.]]
